node-2.label: 65-year-old man with no reported medical history, no treatment at home, completely self-sufficient before admission, arrived at ICU intubated and mechanically ventilated due to loss of consciousness with Glasgow Coma Scale rapidly deteriorating to 3

node-3.label: After initial treatment and recovery, patient experienced multiple complications including acute respiratory distress syndrome, septic shock events, cardiogenic shock, obstructive shock due to pulmonary embolism, and multi-organ failure requiring hemodialysis

node-4.label: On day 39 of ICU care, after stabilization and lifting of sedation, examination revealed spontaneous eye opening without contact, no motor response, and basic neurological status with no meaningful interaction

why.why: Acute GCS 3, severe shock/ARDS, and post-sedation wakefulness without awareness remain strong clinical support for hypoxic-ischemic brain injury. However, initial CT/MRI showed only a right posterior inferior cerebellar artery territory infarct without the classic hypoxic-ischemic pattern, and follow-up MRI on day 49 showed no new parenchymal lesions; EEG improved from non-reactive delta to reactive theta, suggesting partial cerebral recovery. These findings make diffuse hypoxic-ischemic injury less typical, so confidence is slightly lowered to 0.72, though it remains the leading hypothesis.

Early coma and sepsis initially supported toxic-metabolic encephalopathy, but persistence after stabilization and sedation withdrawal, along with EEG evolution to reactive theta and no new MRI lesions, argues against an ongoing toxic-metabolic cause. Expert analyses agree that toxic-metabolic encephalopathy is less likely after stabilization, so confidence is lowered to 0.10.
